questions.question: Read the passage about Dexter, a German General in the Second World War, and answer: who was Dexter?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Dexter was a **Military General in Hitler's army** during the Second World War.

**What the passage tells us about him.** He was appointed the Guard of a fortress near the French border, and his wife was left behind to be "the hostage of the hostage" — a guarantee of his loyalty — if he failed in his duties there. When the Allied Army attacked continuously and his ten thousand German soldiers were left without ammunition, without medicine and without treatment, Dexter faced a choice between fighting on and surrendering.

**Supporting details for a longer answer.** He received a letter telling him that his wife would be dead of cancer by the time he returned, which removed the last reason for holding out; he thereupon killed his immediate commanders, announced the surrender on radio, and saved the lives of the ten thousand men, who were then cared for by Allied doctors.

**Marking note.** "German Military General under Hitler" earns the mark; adding "appointed Guard of a fortress near the French border" shows full comprehension.

questions.question: Read the passage about Dexter, a German General in the Second World War, and answer: when and where was he appointed?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** He was appointed **during the Second World War**, as the **Guard of a fortress near the French border**.

**The words of the passage.**

> "Dexter was a Military General in Hitler's Army. During the second world war he was appointed as the Guard of a fourtress near the French border."

**One-line answer for the booklet.** During the Second World War, Dexter was appointed the Guard of a fortress near the French border.

**Note on the source text.** The printed passage spells "fortress" as "fourtress"; in your answer use the normal spelling.

questions.question: Read the passage about Dexter and answer: what was the concern for his wife?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** His wife was being held as a **hostage** — she would be treated as a hostage if the General failed in his duties. His constant worry was what would become of her, and this is the "confusion" that filled his mind.

**The two layers of the worry.**

1. **Political:** she had been left behind as security for his loyalty, so any failure on his part would cost her her freedom, perhaps her life.
2. **Personal:** in the middle of the siege he received a letter saying that she would be **dead of cancer** by the time he returned home.

**How it decided his action.** Once he knew his wife was lost anyway, "there was now nothing to be afraid of or to care for" — the hostage-hold had no meaning left, and he announced the surrender.

**Model two-mark answer.** Dexter's wife had been left behind as a hostage who would suffer if he failed in his duty, and he was deeply anxious about her fate. A letter then told him that she would die of cancer before he could return, and this grief, added to the hopeless military position, decided his surrender.

questions.question: Read the passage about Dexter and answer: why were the German soldiers helpless?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The German soldiers were helpless because, after the continuous attack of the Allied Army, only ten thousand of them were left, **without any ammunition**, and they were "in the most miserable condition with all the injuries but no medicines and no treatment".

**The four reasons, one by one.**

1. **Continuous attack** by the Allied Army had worn them down.
2. **No ammunition** — they could not fire back.
3. **No medicine and no treatment** — the wounded could not be cared for.
4. **A call for total surrender** — the Allies announced "support for their surrender" and Hitler wanted everyone to die on the battlefield rather than give in.

**Model two-mark answer.** Continuous attacks by the Allied Army had left only ten thousand German soldiers, all of them out of ammunition. With no medicines and no treatment for their injuries and no possibility of resistance, they could neither fight nor save their wounded — hence their helplessness.

questions.question: Read the passage about Dexter and answer: why did Dexter announce the surrender?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Dexter announced the surrender because, after receiving his wife's letter, **"there was now nothing to be afraid of or to care for"** — the hostage threat that had kept him fighting had lost its power.

**The chain of reasoning.**

- He was holding a hopeless position: no ammunition, no medicine, wounded men everywhere.
- He had hesitated to surrender because his wife was a hostage and would suffer if he failed.
- The letter told him she would be **dead of cancer** before his return — so nothing remained that his surrender could injure.
- He therefore **killed his immediate commanders**, who would have opposed him, and announced the surrender on the radio.

**Model two-mark answer.** Dexter had been afraid to surrender because his wife was held as a hostage and would be punished for his failure. When a letter informed him that she would die of cancer before his return, there was nothing left for him to fear or to protect. He killed his immediate officers, who would have stopped him, and announced the surrender, thereby saving ten thousand lives.

questions.question: Read the passage about Dexter and answer: what was the advantage of surrender?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The advantage was that the **ten thousand surviving soldiers were looked after by the doctors of the Allied Army and got the chance "to survive and to live on"**.

**Contrast the two outcomes.**

| If he had fought on | After surrender |
|---|---|
| Ten thousand men with no ammunition, no medicine, no treatment would have been wiped out | Allied doctors treated their injuries |
| Hitler demanded that everyone die on the battlefield | The men "got the chance to survive and to live on" |

**Model two-mark answer.** By surrendering, Dexter saved ten thousand lives. The wounded were treated by Allied Army doctors instead of being left without medicine or care, and the soldiers were given the chance to survive and live — something that continuing the hopeless fight would have denied them.

questions.question: Read the passage about Dexter and answer: explain the word 'Hostage'.
questions.answer:
**Answer.** A **hostage** is a person who is held by one party as a guarantee that the other party will keep a promise, surrender, or behave in a particular way; if the promise is broken, the hostage may be harmed.

**In the passage.** Dexter's wife was left behind as a hostage: if the General failed in his duties at the fortress, she would be the one to suffer.

**Marking note.** The definition needs two elements to be complete: (i) a person held or detained, and (ii) as security for the good conduct or promise of another. Synonyms such as "captive" or "pawn" may be added.

**An example** helps in one-mark answers: "The hijackers held the passengers hostage until their demands were met."

questions.question: Read the passage beginning 'The human being is the most unique of all the creatures…' and find the important points in the passage.
questions.answer:
**Important points (notes)**

**1. Human being — most unique**
   1.1 Power of reasoning and logic
   1.2 Helpless at the start (parasite on the parental plant)

**2. Behaviour of a slave**
   2.1 A slave to the senior members around
   2.2 A slave to his own desires and wishes

**3. Points of growth**
   3.1 School and other points of growth
   3.2 Feeling of novelty in life
   3.3 Web of the family — children, duties and liabilities

**4. Towards old age**
   4.1 Time takes long strides
   4.2 The mirror shows the stamp on the face — lines and wrinkles
   4.3 Old age arrives as a bundle of diseases

**5. The struggle**
   5.1 Struggle starts at life
   5.2 A moment when the story closes
   5.3 Life becomes past

**6. Central idea (in one line)**
   6.1 From helpless infancy through servitude and growth to old age and death, human life is a continuous struggle

**Marking scheme reminder.** Notes must be in **headings and sub-headings** with abbreviated, keyword-style entries — not full sentences — and numbered consistently. The examiner looks first for the structure, then for coverage of the passage's stages of life.

questions.question: Read the passage beginning 'The human being is the most unique of all the creatures…' and write the summary in fifty words.
questions.answer:
**Summary (about 50 words).**

Man is the most unique creature, gifted with reason and logic, yet he begins life utterly helpless, dependent on his parents. He then becomes a slave to elders and to his own desires, passes through school, family duties and liabilities, and finally reaches old age — lines, wrinkles and diseases — where life closes and becomes the past. Life is a continuous struggle.

**Why this summary works.**

- It follows the **order of the passage**: uniqueness → helpless infancy → slavery to desires → growth and family → old age → death.
- It keeps the **key images** (parasite on the parental plant; the mirror's "stamp" of lines and wrinkles) in compressed form without quoting at length.
- It is continuous prose, not notes — a summary must read as a paragraph.
- It stays close to 50 words, as the question demands; anything longer loses marks for exceeding the limit.

**A shorter version (45 words), if a tighter limit is preferred.** Man is unique in his reasoning but starts life helpless, a parasite on his parents. He grows into a slave of elders and of his own wishes, passes through school and family duties, and ends in old age — wrinkles, diseases and death. Life is one long struggle.

questions.question: You have lost your keys in the college campus. Write a notice for the notice-board.
questions.answer:
**JAIN MODEL COLLEGE, PAKUR**

**NOTICE**

**28 February 2013**

**LOST — A BUNCH OF KEYS**

A bunch of keys was lost in the college campus during the break today. The bunch has a bike-key and a key with an "A"-shaped ring. The finder is requested to return it to the undersigned. A suitable reward is promised.

**Abhishek Tiwari**
Class XII-A, Roll No. 104

**Format checklist.**

1. **NOTICE** at the top, centred, with the institution's name above it.
2. **Date** of issue below the heading (the date matters — the notice is time-bound).
3. A **caption** in capitals: "LOST — A BUNCH OF KEYS".
4. **Body**: what was lost, distinguishing features (bike-key, "A"-shaped ring), where and when, and what the finder should do.
5. **Signature and designation** of the writer at the bottom left.
6. **50 words**, boxed. No salutation, no address of the writer beyond class and roll number.

**Note on the printed model.** The booklet's answer is headed "28 Feb 2013 / NOTICE" and closes "A treat is promised" — a reward, in student language. Either "a suitable reward" or "a treat" is acceptable, but keep one, not both.

questions.question: You have organised a cultural programme in your college. Write a notice inviting the names of the participants.
questions.answer:
**CULTURAL CLUB**
**HAPPY CHILD PUBLIC SCHOOL, JAMSHEDPUR**

**NOTICE**

**10 March 2013**

**GRAND CULTURAL EVENING — INVITATION TO PARTICIPATE**

The Cultural Club is organising a grand Cultural Evening on 15 March 2013 at 6 p.m. in the school auditorium, as a thanksgiving programme on the last working day of the session. Students of Class XII will present a short dance-drama on "Chandalika" by Tagore; Bharatanatyam, poetic recitation and group songs will be the other attractions. Students willing to participate should give their names to the undersigned by 12 March 2013. Participants must report five minutes before the programme begins. Sorry, guests will not be entertained.

**Rajeev**
Secretary, Cultural Club

**Format checklist.**

- Institution and issuing body at the top; **NOTICE** and the **date** prominently displayed.
- A **caption** in capitals.
- Body answering: **what** (cultural evening), **when** (15 March, 6 p.m.), **where** (school auditorium), **who may participate** (students of Class XII), **what they must do** (give names by 12 March), and any **conditions** (report five minutes early; no guests).
- **Signature with designation** at the bottom.
- Within the word limit, inside a box.

**Why the details earn marks.** A notice is an *instruction*, so the examiner rewards completeness — a missing last date or venue means the reader cannot act on it.

questions.question: Write a letter to the Branch Manager, SBI, Patna requesting him to consider your request for a job.
questions.answer:
**Puja Sharma**
66-A, B.D. Road, Kuju

**20 March 2013**

**To
The Branch Manager
State Bank of India
Patna**

**Sub: Application for the post of Clerk**

**Sir**

Kindly refer to your advertisement in *Hindustan Times* dated 15 March 2013, inviting applications for the post of clerk in your branch. I wish to be considered for the said post.

My bio-data is enclosed for your kind consideration. I am a graduate of Ranchi University and hold a diploma in Computer Applications from BIT, and I have one year's experience. If found suitable, I shall be glad to appear for an interview at any time convenient to you. In case of selection, I assure you of my unstinted co-operation and devotion in the discharge of my duties.

**Yours faithfully**
**Puja Sharma**

**Encl.: Bio-data**

**BIO-DATA**

| | |
|---|---|
| Name | Puja Sharma |
| Father's name | Prof. M.N. Sharma |
| Address | 66-A, B.D. Road, Kuju |
| Date of birth | 15 September 1985 |
| Educational qualification | (i) B.Com., Ranchi University (ii) Diploma in Computer Application, BIT |
| Experience | 1 year |
| Marital status | Unmarried |
| References | 1. Prof. G. Mohan, R.U. 2. Prof. C. Ranjan, B.I.T. |

**Format checklist for a formal application.**

1. Sender's address, then **date**.
2. Receiver's designation and address.
3. **Subject line** in one sentence.
4. Salutation "Sir/Madam" (not "Dear sir" in an Indian formal letter of application), body, and "Yours faithfully".
5. **Enclosure** noted at the foot, with the bio-data in tabular form giving name, father's name, address, date of birth, qualifications, experience, marital status and references.

questions.question: Write a letter to your Principal requesting him to grant you books from the library for a period of six months.
questions.answer:
**Rahul Jha**
Class XII-A, Roll No. 185
Jai Narain Public School, Jhansi

**7 September 2013**

**To
The Principal
Jai Narain Public School
Jhansi**

**Sub: Request for granting books from the library for six months**

**Sir**

I am a student of the science stream of Class XII of your school. We have been given a physics project to prepare for the inter-state science fair to be held next month.

For this purpose we need to use some important books from our school library, as our teachers have advised. These books are not available in the open market, and we require them continuously for reference and experiment. I therefore request you to kindly grant us these books from the library for a period of six months.

I shall be grateful for your kind consideration and shall return the books in good condition within the stipulated period.

**Yours obediently**
**Rahul Jha**
Class XII-A, Roll No. 185

**Format checklist.**

1. Sender's address, **date**, receiver's address.
2. **Subject line** naming the exact request.
3. Body in three parts: the reason (project for the science fair), the request (books for six months), and the assurance (return in good condition).
4. "Yours obediently" (appropriate for a pupil writing to a Principal) or "Yours faithfully".
5. Courteous tone throughout — a request letter never demands.

**Why the reason matters.** A Principal grants an unusual loan only if the purpose is clear, so the science-fair justification and the teachers' advice must be stated explicitly.

questions.question: Write a report on the election scene in your locality.
questions.answer:
**ELECTION FEVER GRIPS RANCHI MUNICIPALITY**

**By a Staff Reporter**
**Ranchi, 14 April 2013**

Municipal elections were held in Ranchi municipality recently for 55 wards and for the office of Mayor. There were busy roads, colourful banners and long queues at the polling booths throughout the day.

The candidates had been busy for weeks. Their supporters went from door to door, organising meetings and making the community aware of local issues. The roads of every ward carried hoardings and posters, and the small tea shops were full of gossip about the elections. On polling day itself, voters queued patiently from early morning; by evening the turnout was reported to be high.

For the roadside boys, election time meant good days: they were paid regularly by the leaders until the election day, and many of them found work carrying flags and leaflets.

The results were declared two days later. The contest was keen in several wards, and the new councillors have promised better roads, water supply and drainage. The administration has thanked the voters for a peaceful poll.

**Format checklist.**

1. **Headline** in capitals, then **by-line** and **place-date**.
2. Opening paragraph: **what, where, when, who**.
3. Middle paragraphs: the run-up (campaigning, posters, gossip), then polling day (queues, turnout).
4. Closing paragraph: results and consequences.
5. Third person, past tense, no "I/we" — and no opinion; a report states facts.

**Mark-earning details.** Specifics such as 55 wards, the office of Mayor, hoardings, tea-shop gossip and the paid helpers give the report its texture.

questions.question: Write a report on a journey recently experienced by you.
questions.answer:
**AN INTERESTING JOURNEY BY TRAIN**

**By Rahul Jha**
**7 September 2013**

It was a Wednesday morning when I boarded the train for Chennai from Ranchi station. I had a reservation in coach No. 2, and to my surprise the compartment was full and yet comfortable.

My companions were a very nice and accommodating family with two children. As the train moved from station to station the pitch and tempo of conversation rose. We had packed breakfast brought from home, and it was taken for granted that all of us would share one another's food — a small courtesy that turned strangers into friends at once.

Three hours passed without our noticing the distance travelled, and we all alighted feeling as though we had been a happy family for years. We exchanged addresses at the platform.

The journey taught me something I have not forgotten: if the whole of India could share a compartment in this spirit, there would be far less conflict in the country. I wished the train had been the whole country, where all Indians could care for one another and share the joys and sorrows of life together.

**Format checklist.**

1. **Headline**, by-line and date.
2. A **chronological** account: boarding → the compartment → the family → conversation and food → arrival.
3. One **reflective closing paragraph** — in a personal report an observation is allowed, and here it supplies the point of the piece.
4. Past tense, first person is acceptable because the report describes *your* journey (contrast the impersonal election report).

**Note on the printed model.** The booklet's answer is headed "An Interesting Journey By Train" and ends with the wish that the compartment were the whole of India — reproduce that thought, but in correct, complete sentences.

questions.question: Write an article on 'Ambition in Life'.
questions.answer:
**AMBITION IN LIFE**

Every person should have an ambition in life. Life is like a breakless vehicle which cannot go on without any ambition. An ambition gives direction, a way to grow up for one's future — a goal, a focus, a reason to work.

An ambition encourages a person to work hard and to do well in the field he has dreamt of. A student who wishes to become a doctor studies biology with a different seriousness from one who has no aim; the same study, but a different energy. Ambition is thus the engine of effort: without it, talent remains idle.

An ambitious person is also very good for the country. He is the best human resource of his nation. Ambitious doctors, engineers, teachers, farmers and scientists build a strong nation, because each of them tries not only to earn a living but to do his work better than it has been done before.

The ambition must, however, be honest and realistic. An ambition for money alone narrows the mind; an ambition for excellence enlarges it. The young should choose an aim that uses their abilities and serves others, then pursue it with patience, for achievement comes to those who keep working after others have tired.

**Format checklist.**

1. **Title** in capitals.
2. **Introduction** — the necessity of ambition.
3. **Body** — what ambition does for the individual, then for the nation.
4. **Conclusion** — a qualifying remark (ambition must be honest and realistic) plus an appeal to the young.
5. **150 words**, formal and impersonal, with concrete illustrations rather than vague statements.

questions.question: Write an article on 'Discipline in Life'.
questions.answer:
**DISCIPLINE IN LIFE**

Discipline is essential in life. Without discipline, life is like an animal's life. Human beings are called human beings because of discipline: it is the necessary element of our existence.

We learn discipline at every step, in every habit of life. A child learns to sleep and wake at fixed hours, to greet elders, to wait for his turn; a student learns to sit at his books at the appointed time; a player obeys the rules of his game. Discipline makes us behave with appropriate manners, and without it life would be a hell.

Discipline begins in the home and the school. It is in the family that a boy first learns obedience and self-control, and it is in school that he learns regularity, punctuality and respect for rules. Later, discipline becomes the basis of success in every profession: a doctor cannot save a life, nor a soldier defend a border, without it.

Discipline is not slavery. It is the voluntary control of one's desires in the service of a chosen aim — the very thing that separates a human being from an animal. A disciplined life is therefore a free life, for it is ruled by purpose and not by impulse.

**Format checklist.**

1. **Title** in capitals.
2. **Introduction** stating the thesis (discipline distinguishes man from beast).
3. **Body**: where discipline is learnt (home, school) and where it is needed (profession, national life), with examples.
4. **Conclusion** answering a possible objection: discipline is self-control, not slavery.
5. **150 words**, formal register, no personal anecdotes in an article of this kind.

questions.question: Read the lines beginning 'Aunt Jennifer's finger fluttering through her wool…' and answer: why are the fingers fluttering?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The fingers are fluttering because Aunt Jennifer is **nervous and afraid** — the "massive weight of Uncle's wedding band" sits heavily on her hand, and her fingers can hardly push the needle through.

**What the lines say.**

> "Aunt Jennifer's finger fluttering through her wool / Find even the ivory needle hard to pull / The massive weight of Uncle's wedding band / Sits heavily upon Aunt Jennifer's hand."

**Why the fluttering matters.** The trembling is not the ordinary clumsiness of an embroiderer: it is the physical sign of a life of fear and repression inside marriage. The needle that should move easily ("hard to pull") shows how even the smallest act of creation is a strain for her.

**One-mark answer.** Her fingers are fluttering because she is old, nervous and frightened, and the heavy wedding ring on her hand makes even the simple act of pulling the ivory needle difficult.

questions.question: Read the lines beginning 'Aunt Jennifer's finger fluttering through her wool…' and answer: why can the needle not be pulled?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The needle cannot be pulled because the **"massive weight of Uncle's wedding band"** sits heavily upon Aunt Jennifer's hand, hampering the free movement of her fingers.

**Two readings, both correct.**

1. **Literal:** the ring is physically heavy — the marriage band weighs down the hand, and her trembling fingers cannot manage the small, precise movement needed.
2. **Symbolic:** the ring stands for the burden of a joyless marriage; the "weight" is the weight of male domination, which cripples her will as it cripples her needlework.

**One-mark answer.** The heavy wedding ring — symbol of an oppressive marriage — weighs down her hand, so her trembling fingers cannot pull the ivory needle through the wool.

questions.question: Read the lines beginning 'Aunt Jennifer's finger fluttering through her wool…' and answer: why is the wedding band a weight?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The wedding band is a weight because it stands for a **loveless, oppressive marriage** that has burdened and crushed Aunt Jennifer's spirit throughout her life.

**How the poem makes the point.**

- The ring is called "**massive**" and "**heavy**" — adjectives of physical burden applied to a symbol.
- It is "**Uncle's** wedding band", not hers — she wears a token of someone else's authority.
- It cripples her art: the needle "hard to pull", the fingers "fluttering".
- In death the ring is still with her: "the **ordeals** she was mastered by" will lie upon her hands as she lies in her grave.

**One-mark answer.** The wedding band is a weight because it symbolises the heavy, crushing burden of an unhappy marriage, which has controlled her life and left her afraid even of her own creativity.

questions.question: Why does the poetess smile at the time when she leaves her elderly mother? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** She smiles to **hide her pain and fear**. As a child she had known the "old familiar ache" of parting, and now the sight of her ageing mother brings it back. The smile is an attempt "to hide the ache and hide inside the heart".

**What the poem says exactly.**

> "…and all I did was smile and smile and smile…"
> "…the old familiar ache, my childhood's fear, / But all I said was, see you soon, Amma…"

**The three things she is doing at once.**

1. **Reassuring her mother** — "see you soon, Amma" is a promise, not a farewell.
2. **Concealing her own fear** — the repeated "smile and smile and smile" is a mask, the smile of a person who dare not speak what she feels.
3. **Refusing to name death** — to say aloud that her mother looks "like a corpse" would be unbearable, so she smiles instead.

**Model two-mark answer.** The poetess smiles because she cannot bear to show her fear. The sight of her mother's ashen, corpse-like face reminds her of her approaching death and revives the "old familiar ache" of childhood partings. Saying "see you soon, Amma", she smiles and smiles again to hide the pain inside her heart.

questions.question: Why is Jennifer afraid of lying in the grave? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** She is afraid that **even death will not free her from Uncle's control**: the wedding band and "the ordeals she was mastered by" will still be with her in the grave.

**The closing lines of the poem.**

> "When Aunt is dead, her terrified hands will lie / Still ringed with ordeals she was mastered by."

**What "terrified" tells us.** It is not dying that terrifies Aunt Jennifer — it is that death, which should bring release, brings none. The ring remains on her finger after she dies; the mastery of her husband outlasts her body. Death, for her, is simply one more place where she must belong to Uncle.

**Contrast with the tigers.** The tigers she embroiders are "not afraid" and "proud" and will "go on prancing, proud and unafraid" for ever. The tigers are the freedom she cannot have, in life or in death.

**Model two-mark answer.** Jennifer fears the grave because she believes that even there she will remain in her husband's power. Her "terrified hands will lie still ringed with ordeals she was mastered by" — the wedding band and the memory of domination will accompany her into death, so that dying offers her no escape.

questions.question: Where is the small boy lost in the slum school? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The small boy is "lost in a **dark, dumb room**" of the slum school — a room from which the sun's light, the sky and the freedom outside have been shut out by the school building itself.

**The words of the poem.**

> "…the little boy / Who sits at the back of the dim class, / … is lost in a dark, dumb room."

The schoolroom is described as "dark" and "dumb": it admits no light and offers no language other than the hopeless map on the wall.

**What the image means.**

- The "map" on the wall advertises "the world" — oceans, forests, cities — but the boy has never seen any of it.
- The windows are "grey", the sun's beam is "shut out" by the school-building itself.
- He is "lost" not in space but in his own life: he cannot even "observe the root of the tree" he plays near, and his dreams are of "the squirrel's game" rather than of anything the classroom offers.

**Model two-mark answer.** The small boy is at the back of the dim, dark classroom of the slum school, sitting in a "dark, dumb room" whose windows admit no sunlight. The school carries the visible world only as a map on the wall; the boy himself is lost in it, untouched by the world that education is supposed to open.

questions.question: Write the story of the Rattrap.
questions.answer:
**The metaphor.** The peddler, a ragged man who sells small rattraps made of wire, has come to see the world itself as a giant rattrap: "all through the story he had been thinking of the world as a rattrap". Its baits are food, clothes, shelter and money. Once a man takes the bait, the trap "closes in on him and then everything comes to an end".

**The story.** On a cold December night he is given shelter and hospitality by an old crofter, a lonely man who shows him his **thirty kronor** kept in a leather pouch. The next morning the peddler breaks open the pouches and steals the money.

He loses his way in the forest and, after wandering, is taken up by an **ironmaster** who mistakes him for an old comrade, Nils Olof, and treats him royally, giving him clothes and food. When the error is discovered the ironmaster wants to call the sheriff, but his daughter **Edla** persuades her father to let the man stay for Christmas. She treats him as a real guest, with "deep sympathy, kindness, love and understanding".

Under that warmth the peddler's conscience wakes. He cannot bear his own disgrace and slips out before dawn, leaving for Edla a small Christmas packet, with a letter and a gift: the **three wrinkled ten-kronor notes** and a request that the money be returned to the crofter, from "a little rat who would have been caught in the world's trap had he not been raised to a captain". Edla's kindness has saved him: the rattrap had been baited, but the man escaped.

**Model 125-word answer.** A peddler of wire rattraps, who believed the world was a rattrap whose baits are food, shelter and money, took shelter one Christmas night with a lonely crofter and stole his thirty kronor. Lost in the forest, he was mistaken by an ironmaster for an old friend and, through the kindness of the ironmaster's daughter Edla, treated as a guest rather than a vagrant. Her sympathy and respect woke his conscience. He left before dawn, but left for Edla a Christmas present — the three ten-kronor notes and a letter asking her to return them to the crofter, signed by "a little rat" rescued from the trap. Kindness had raised him, and he escaped the world's rattrap.

questions.question: Write what does Gandhi get from his experience in Champaran.
questions.answer:
**The episode.** The Champaran episode did not begin as an act of defiance: it "grew out of an attempt to remove the distress of large numbers of poor peasants". Gandhi looked into the cause of their suffering and fought the injustice of the landlords, who extracted money from the sharecroppers by forcing them to grow indigo on the best part of their land.

**What Gandhi got from the experience.**

1. **The first victory of Civil Disobedience in India.** The success of Champaran was a practical proof that non-violent, organised resistance worked against the British.
2. **His first direct contact with the Indian masses.** For the first time he saw at close quarters the poor of the countryside and learnt from them how they "received him", and he valued the goodwill he earned more than the money refunded.
3. **A lasting lesson in legal morale.** The sharecroppers got back only twenty-five per cent of the money they had paid, but what mattered more was that the **English landlords had to surrender part of their money and with it part of their prestige**. Previously they had behaved as though above the law; now the peasants "saw that they had rights and defenders".
4. **Leadership and humility.** He learnt that a moral cause can be won by patience — accepting a compromise, refusing a good name for himself, and organising schools and health care.
5. **A turning point he himself recognised.** Gandhi "himself accepts that the Champaran episode was a turning point in his life": it taught him that India lived in its villages and that the common people could be organised non-violently.

**Model 125-word answer.** In Champaran, where English landlords forced sharecroppers to grow indigo and extorted money from them, Gandhi began with an attempt to remove the distress of the poor. From his investigation and the movement that followed he obtained his first victory of Civil Disobedience in India. He learnt that the peasants, once shown a defender, gained courage: the landlords surrendered not merely part of the refund but part of their prestige, and the peasants came to see that they had rights. He also learnt the value of patience, of a muddled economy of means, and of the goodwill of the crowd. The twenty-five per cent refund meant less than the moral victory. He accepted this episode as a turning point in his life and in freedom-fighting methods in India.

questions.question: Write how does Sadao help the American soldier.
questions.answer:
**The situation.** Dr Sadao Hoki finds a wounded American prisoner of war thrown up on the beach near his house. Though Japan is at war with America, he cannot leave the man to die — "the man will die" — and his neighbours will call it a "nightmare" if he is found.

**What Sadao does, step by step.**

1. **He carries the man home** with his wife Hana, and orders the servants — who grumble and eventually leave — to treat him as a patient.
2. **He operates** on the man on the mat in the guest room, removes the bullet, and then spends anxious days nursing him. The servants' departure leaves Hana to do the work of the household alone.
3. **He protects him**, refusing to hand him over to the police and finally reporting the matter to the General (who promises to send assassins who never arrive).
4. **He equips him to escape.** He puts food, bottled water and two quilts into a boat, gives the American a **new life at the age of twenty-five**, and instructs him to row to a deserted island nearby, wait there, and from there signal for help from a Korean fishing boat: "food… bottled water and two quilts were put inside the boat".
5. **He tells the man exactly how to escape:** the American is to row to a deserted island nearby and wait there, and when he sees a Korean fishing boat pass by he must "signal two flashes" with a torch. He is warned never to signal in darkness, since he would then be spotted.

So Sadao helps by **healing him, sheltering him, and finally setting him free**, thereby choosing the duty of a doctor and the claim of humanity over the demands of wartime patriotism.

**Model 125-word answer.** When Sadao finds a wounded American prisoner on the beach, he brings him home with Hana and, in spite of the danger to his own household, treats him as a patient. He operates to remove the bullet and nurses him slowly to recovery. He does not hand the fugitive over to the police and reports the matter only to the General, who promises action and never sends it. When the man is well, Sadao decides to set him free: he gives him a boat, food, bottled water and two quilts, and tells him to row to a nearby deserted island and wait there out of sight until he can signal to a Korean fishing boat passing by. He warns him never to signal in darkness. Mercy and the doctor's duty win over patriotic hatred.

questions.question: Write the summary of the Tiger King.
questions.answer:
**The prophecy.** The Maharaja of Pratibandapuram is told by an astrologer, on the very day of his birth, that his **death will come from a tiger**. The bull and the Tiger, the astrologer explains, are born enemies — as the bull is his birth sign, the Tiger will bring his death. The boy grows up to be a proud, strong and ruthless king known as the Tiger King.

**The campaign.** When he becomes king he resolves to kill every tiger in his state, and more: he forbids the killing of tigers by anyone else, forbids even the shooting of magic arrows at them, and confiscates the property of any subject who crosses the decree. Tigers being scarce, he marries into a royal family whose state is rich in tigers, and kills them there as well. He reaches **ninety-nine** in ten years of hunting.

**The hundredth tiger.** A tiger is finally sighted, already old and ill; the Maharaja shoots at it and the animal **faints** with shock, not from the bullet. Afraid to tell him the truth, the hunters kill the tiger and report that it was his shot that did it. The Maharaja is "overcome with elation", orders the dead tiger to be brought to the capital in a grand procession, buries it beneath a mound and builds a tomb over it.

**The irony.** Two days later he buys his son a **wooden toy tiger** from the village toy-seller. While playing with it a **silver sliver** from the cheap toy pierces his right hand. Infection spreads; the surgeon says, "The operation was successful. The Maharaja is dead." Thus the hundredth tiger "took its revenge upon the Tiger King" — and the prophecy is fulfilled, not by a tiger of flesh and blood but by a wooden one.

**Model 125-word answer.** The Maharaja of Pratibandapuram was told at birth that his death would come from a tiger, and he grew up into a proud hunter-king determined to disprove fate. He killed ninety-nine tigers and became famous for it, banning all others from killing or even shooting magic arrows at tigers and marrying into a state where tigers were plentiful. When the hundredth tiger appeared, the ageing animal merely fainted at his shot and was finished off by others, but his people reported that the king had killed it. He celebrated with a procession and a tomb. Not long afterwards, playing with a cheap wooden toy tiger bought for his son, he was pierced by a silver sliver in it; the wound turned septic and killed him. The hundredth tiger had its revenge.

questions.question: How does Franz change his feelings about Mr. Hamel? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Before.** Franz was afraid of Mr. Hamel and hated his hard manner: the teacher's iron ruler, the "cranky" temper, the dreaded questions on participles. He even thought of skipping school to avoid the scolding.

**After the last lesson.** Everything changes once Franz learns that the German teacher has been ordered to leave Alsace:

- **"My books, that had seemed such a nuisance a while ago, so heavy to carry, my grammar, and my history of the saints, were old friends now that I couldn't give up."**
- He now feels **pity** for M. Hamel — "the idea that this was the last time he would see him made him forget all about his crankiness and his ruler."
- He notices the old man's **sorrow and dignity**: the pale face, the effort to sit upright, and finally the silent writing of "Vive La France!" on the blackboard.

**The change in one sentence.** Fear and resentment turn into respect and affection: the hated schoolmaster becomes a tragic figure whose sacrifice for the language gives him greatness.

**Model two-mark answer.** At first Franz feared and disliked M. Hamel for his strictness and his ruler. When the order from Berlin came, he saw the same teacher with new eyes: the master was leaving, and with him the French language; his books became old friends, and Franz pitied rather than feared him. Respect and affection replaced his old indifference.

questions.question: Describe the hardships working in the bangle industry. (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**The answer (from the chapter).** Working in the glass bangle industry is "hazardous":

1. **Extreme heat** — the bangle-makers sit in glass furnaces at very high temperatures, for long hours.
2. **Poor lighting** — they work in dingy cells **without air and light**, so their eyes have to adjust from the dark furnace to the bright daylight outside.
3. **Loss of eyesight** — this constant strain causes many of them to **lose their eyesight before they become adults**.
4. **Economic exploitation** — they earn very little for the glass bangles they make, work as virtual slaves of middlemen, and suffer cold, hunger and squalor.

**The chapter's sentence to quote.** "The bangle makers of Firozabad work in glass furnaces with high temperatures, in dingy cells without air and light."

**Model two-mark answer.** The bangle-makers of Firozabad work at blazing furnaces in hot, airless cells where there is no light, so that their eyes must adjust between furnace and daylight. The result is that many lose their eyesight even before they reach adulthood. Wages are pitiful and the workers are trapped by middlemen, so their labour is both eye-destroying and exploitative.

questions.question: How does Edla change the character of the Peddler? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**The answer.** Edla is the "ironmaster's daughter who proves an angel in the peddler's life". By treating him as a human being rather than a vagrant, she wakes his conscience and restores his self-respect.

**How she does it.**

1. **She protests when her father wants to throw him out** — she persuades the ironmaster to let the man stay for Christmas and to keep the mistake to themselves.
2. **She treats him as a real guest** — "she treated him as a real captain", giving him food, warmth and attention, and covering her own shame at her father's harshness.
3. **She offers him kindness where others offered suspicion** — "the deep sympathy, kindness, love and understanding in Edla's eyes" transform him.
4. **He responds by becoming honest.** He leaves her a Christmas present: the three wrinkled ten-kronor notes stolen from the crofter, and a letter asking her to return them. He signs himself "a little rat" who would have been caught in the world's rattrap had he not been "raised to a captain" — the "captain" being Edla's elevation of him.

**Model two-mark answer.** Edla changes the peddler by her sympathy and respect. When her father discovers the mistake, she persuades him not to turn the man out and treats the peddler as a genuine guest, with kindness and understanding. Moved by this, the peddler's conscience revives: he leaves behind the stolen thirty kronor and a letter asking her to return the money to the crofter, and calls himself a "little rat" saved by being treated as a captain.

questions.question: How does Douglas learn swimming? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**The answer.** After nearly drowning at the age of ten in the Yakima pool, Douglas is left with a terror of water. He learns to swim later by hiring an **instructor** and practising the techniques in stages.

**The steps.**

1. **Getting rid of the old terror** — the instructor builds a rope through a pulley over the pool with a belt round Douglas's waist, so that he is held up and cannot drown: "the instructor put a rope through a pulley on an overhead cable".
2. **Breathing practice** — he is made to **exhale under water and inhale when the face came up**, again and again, until it became automatic.
3. **Kicking at the edge** — he is made to kick with his legs at the edge of the pool, hundreds of times, "till the instructor built a swimmer" out of him.
4. **Integration** — each piece is then joined into a single smooth action, so that by the end he can swim the length of the pool, dive and surface.
5. **Testing the conquest** — he goes alone to Lake Wentworth and swims across to the other shore, then to Warm Lake, to prove that the fear had been conquered.

**Model two-mark answer.** Douglas engaged an instructor who first removed his terror by fixing a rope and belt so that he could not drown. He taught him to exhale under water and inhale as he raised his face, and had him kick at the edge of the pool hundreds of times. Piece by piece the movements were joined into a single act, and Douglas learned to swim. Later he swam alone across Lake Wentworth to prove that his fear was finally conquered.

questions.question: When does Sophie see Danny Casey in person? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**The answer.** Sophie **never** actually sees Danny Casey in person. She only **imagines** meeting him.

**What happens in the story.**

1. Sophie goes to watch a football match, sees Casey play, and on the way home constructs her fantasy: she meets him in the arcade behind the Royce Street shops and talks with him by the canal.
2. Later she tells Geoff that Casey asked her to meet him again, and when she goes to the appointed place **he does not come** — she waits, watching the canal, and only imagines his figure.
3. The "meeting" is described with all the detail of a real one: "the green of the street lamp", the bicycle, the "brilliant" player — but it is a product of her dreaming.

**Where she does see him.** Only on the **field**, as a footballer among the other players; the personal encounter exists nowhere outside her imagination.

**Model two-mark answer.** Sophie does not meet Danny Casey in person at all: her encounter in the arcade and at the canal is pure imagination. She sees him only as a footballer on the field during a match, and when she waits for the promised meeting by the canal he never comes.

questions.question: What is the meaning of Sam's letter to Charley? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**The answer.** Sam's letter — posted from **Galesburg, Illinois, dated 18 July 1894** — is proof that Sam has **found the third level and escaped into the past**. He writes that he has "found the third level", that he is happy there, and he urges Charley and Louisa to keep looking for it "because now you know it exists".

**What the letter means in the story.**

1. **Confirmation of Charley's experience.** Charley had once strayed on to the third level and seen the 1894 world; Sam's letter proves it was not imagination.
2. **A "first day cover" from the past** — the stamp and postmark belong to 1894, so the letter cannot have come through the normal post; it is a message across time.
3. **A summons.** Sam invites Charley to join him: "I've been here… and I'm not going back." The third level is a refuge from the anxieties of the modern world — the threat of war, insecurity, the "growing like a tree" of Grand Central.
4. **An ironic twist.** The psychiatrist who had called Charley's experience a "waking dream wish fulfilment" himself yields to the same dream, so the story suggests that the wish for a simpler, safer life is universal.

**Model two-mark answer.** Sam's letter, posted from Galesburg on 18 July 1894, means that Sam has himself found the third level and gone back into the past to live there. It confirms that Charley's glimpse of 1894 was real, and it invites Charley and Louisa to keep searching for the third level. The letter — a first day cover of 1894 — is at once proof of escape and a promise that the refuge from the modern world exists.

questions.question: How does the Tiger King die? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**The answer.** He dies of **blood poisoning from a silver sliver in a cheap wooden toy tiger** — not from a real tiger at all.

**How it happens.**

1. On his son's **third birthday** the Maharaja, who had given the boy no time before, goes shopping for a special gift.
2. In a toyshop he finds a **wooden tiger**, made by an unskilled carpenter, with tiny **silver slivers** all over its surface, and buys it as "a perfect gift".
3. The father and son play with the toy; **one sliver pierces the Maharaja's right hand**. He pulls it out, but the wound turns septic and the infection spreads over the whole arm.
4. Three famous surgeons operate, and announce: "**The operation was successful. The Maharaja is dead.**"

**The irony.** The hundredth tiger had been killed — or so he believed — and with it the prophecy. But the prophecy is fulfilled by a **toy** tiger: "the hundredth tiger took its revenge upon the Tiger King". The king who had killed ninety-nine tigers dies of a splinter from a wooden one, and the surgeons' comic verdict mocks the pretence of medical success.

**Model two-mark answer.** The Tiger King dies after a silver sliver from a wooden toy tiger — bought for his son's third birthday — pierces his hand. The wound becomes septic and the infection spreads up his arm; three surgeons operate and report, "The operation was successful. The Maharaja is dead." Thus the hundredth tiger, though only a toy, fulfils the prophecy and takes its revenge.

questions.question: Why is Roger Skunk sad and miserable? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**The answer.** Roger Skunk is sad because **the other little woodland creatures run away from him** — he "smelled so bad" that none of them would play with him.

**What the story tells us.**

- Whenever Roger Skunk went out to play, "all of the other tiny animals would cry, 'Uh-oh, here comes Roger Stinky Skunk'" and they **ran away**.
- "Roger Skunk would stand there all alone, and two little round tears would fall from his eyes."
- His misery drives him to the **owl**, the wise old bird who tells him to go to the wizard, and to the **wizard**, who gives him a spell that makes him smell of roses.

**The deeper point.** His sadness is the pain of exclusion: a child who is different is rejected by the group. The story's conflict begins here — his mother, angry that he now smells of roses and not of a skunk, makes the wizard restore his old smell, because she wants him to remain what he is.

**Model two-mark answer.** Roger Skunk is sad because he smells so bad that the other little animals will not play with him. Whenever he came out, they would shout "here comes Roger Stinky Skunk" and run away, leaving him standing alone with tears rolling down his cheeks. His loneliness sends him to the owl and then to the wizard for a spell that gives him the smell of roses.

questions.question: How does Mr. Lamb die? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**The answer.** Mr. Lamb dies by **falling from a ladder in his garden** while picking apples.

**How it happens in the play.**

1. Derry has run back to the garden, excited by the new understanding that Mr. Lamb has given him, and calls out to him over the garden gate.
2. Mr. Lamb is up a ladder picking apples. As Derry reaches the gate, he hears **"a creak, a crash"** and the **ladder falls backwards**, carrying Mr. Lamb with it: "The branch swished back and he died."
3. Derry's cry — and the silence that follows — confirm that the old man is dead.

**Why the death matters.** It is deliberately off-stage and sudden: the one person who had told Derry that his face did not matter is taken away at the very moment Derry decides to accept himself. The play ends with Derry's grief, and the audience must decide whether the meeting has changed him for good.

**Model two-mark answer.** Mr. Lamb is picking apples from a ladder in his garden when Derry comes running back to see him. As Derry reaches the gate the ladder gives way with a creak and a crash, and the old man falls, striking the ground; the branch swishes back and he dies. His death comes at the very moment Derry has begun to accept himself.
